solution:
[Textbook misprint: the question ends "What must be the magnetic of \(B\)?". The intended word is "magnitude".]

Given: \(m = 20\) g \(= 0.020\) kg, \(L = 1\) m, \(I = 1\) A, and \(\vec{B}\) horizontal and perpendicular to the wire.

To levitate the wire the upward magnetic force must exactly balance its weight:
\(BIL = mg\)
\(\therefore B = \dfrac{mg}{IL} = \dfrac{0.020 \times 9.8}{1 \times 1}\)
\(\therefore B = 0.196\) T

The field must be horizontal and perpendicular to the wire, and oriented so that \(I\vec{L}\times\vec{B}\) points vertically **upward** — reversing either the current or the field would press the wire down instead of lifting it.

Given: \(I = 5\) A, \(d = 2\) cm \(= 0.02\) m, \(\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\) Wb/Am.

For a very long straight wire the magnetic field at a perpendicular distance \(d\) is
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d} = \dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times 5}{2\pi \times 0.02} = \dfrac{2\times10^{-7}\times 5}{0.02}\)
\(\therefore B = 5\times10^{-5}\) T

The field lines are concentric circles around the wire, lying in the plane perpendicular to it; the sense is given by the right-hand grip rule — grasp the wire with the right thumb along the current and the curled fingers give the direction of \(\vec{B}\).

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key reads "3.0 cm, 18.7 MHz, 2.53 keV", and all three values disagree with the question's own data. From \(v = 3.2\times10^{7}\) m/s, \(B = 6.00\times10^{-4}\) T, \(m = 9.1\times10^{-31}\) kg and \(e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\) C the correct values are \(r = 30.3\) cm, \(f = 16.8\) MHz and \(KE = 2.91\) keV. The printed set is also inconsistent with ITSELF: a radius of 3.0 cm at 18.7 MHz implies \(v = 2\pi r f = 3.52\times10^{6}\) m/s and hence a kinetic energy of 0.035 keV, not the 2.53 keV printed beside it. No single choice of the constants reproduces all three printed values.]

Given: \(v = 3.2\times10^{7}\) m/s, \(B = 6.00\times10^{-4}\) T with \(\vec{v}\perp\vec{B}\), \(m = 9.1\times10^{-31}\) kg, \(e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\) C.

**Radius.** The magnetic force supplies the centripetal force:
\(evB = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}\)
\(\therefore r = \dfrac{mv}{eB} = \dfrac{9.1\times10^{-31}\times 3.2\times10^{7}}{1.6\times10^{-19}\times 6.00\times10^{-4}} = \dfrac{2.912\times10^{-23}}{9.6\times10^{-23}}\)
\(\therefore r = 0.303\) m \(= 30.3\) cm

**Frequency.** The cyclotron frequency does not depend on the speed:
\(f = \dfrac{v}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{eB}{2\pi m} = \dfrac{9.6\times10^{-23}}{2\pi \times 9.1\times10^{-31}}\)
\(\therefore f = 1.68\times10^{7}\) Hz \(= 16.8\) MHz

**Kinetic energy.**
\(KE = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\times 9.1\times10^{-31}\times (3.2\times10^{7})^{2} = 4.66\times10^{-16}\) J
\(\therefore KE = \dfrac{4.66\times10^{-16}}{1.6\times10^{-19}} = 2.91\times10^{3}\) eV \(= 2.91\) keV

(At \(v/c \approx 0.107\) the relativistic correction is \(\gamma = 1.006\), i.e. under 1%, so the non-relativistic treatment is appropriate here.)

[Textbook misprint: the question supplies "charge of electron \(= 1.62\times10^{-19}\) C". The accepted value is \(1.60\times10^{-19}\) C, and the book's own printed answer of \(6.643\times10^{-27}\) kg follows from 1.60 and not from 1.62 — the latter would give \(6.72\times10^{-27}\) kg. The working above therefore uses \(1.60\times10^{-19}\) C, which also returns the accepted alpha-particle mass. The stem separately prints "a transverse a uniform magnetic field", with one article too many.]

Given: \(K = 10.00\) MeV, \(B = 1.851\) T, \(r = 24.60\) cm \(= 0.2460\) m, charge of the alpha particle \(q = +2e\).

For a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform field the magnetic force is centripetal, so
\(r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}\quad\Rightarrow\quad mv = qBr\)

The kinetic energy \(K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \dfrac{(mv)^{2}}{2m}\), hence
\(m = \dfrac{(mv)^{2}}{2K} = \dfrac{(qBr)^{2}}{2K}\)

With \(e = 1.60\times10^{-19}\) C: \(q = 2e = 3.2\times10^{-19}\) C and \(K = 10.00\times10^{6}\times 1.6\times10^{-19} = 1.6\times10^{-12}\) J.
\(qBr = 3.2\times10^{-19}\times 1.851 \times 0.2460 = 1.457\times10^{-19}\) kg m/s
\(\therefore m = \dfrac{(1.457\times10^{-19})^{2}}{2\times 1.6\times10^{-12}} = \dfrac{2.123\times10^{-38}}{3.2\times10^{-12}}\)
\(\therefore m = 6.64\times10^{-27}\) kg

This is the accepted mass of the alpha particle (\(6.645\times10^{-27}\) kg, about 4 atomic mass units), which is the check that the working is sound.

[Textbook misprint: the question reads "in apposite directions". The intended word is "opposite", which is what the book's own printed answer of "Repulsive" requires.]

Given: \(I_1 = I_2 = 10\) A in **opposite** directions, separation \(d = 8\) mm \(= 8\times10^{-3}\) m, length of section AB \(= S = 22\) cm \(= 0.22\) m, \(\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\) T m/A.

**Field of wire 2 at the section AB of wire 1.** Wire 2 is long and straight, and AB lies a perpendicular distance \(d\) from it, so
\(B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi d} = \dfrac{2\times10^{-7}\times 10}{8\times10^{-3}}\)
\(\therefore B_2 = 2.5\times10^{-4}\) T

Applying the right-hand grip rule to wire 2 (current flowing downward in the figure) at a point to its left, where wire 1 lies, this field is directed **into the plane of the page**, i.e. perpendicular to the plane containing the two wires.

**Force on wire 1.** The current in AB is upward, perpendicular to \(\vec{B}_2\), so
\(F = B_2 I_1 S = 2.5\times10^{-4}\times 10 \times 0.22\)
\(\therefore F = 5.5\times10^{-4}\) N

Direction: \(\vec{F} = I_1\vec{S}\times\vec{B}_2\) with the current up and \(\vec{B}_2\) into the page gives a force directed **away from wire 2**. Two long parallel wires carrying **antiparallel** currents repel, so the force on wire 1 is **repulsive**, of magnitude \(5.5\times10^{-4}\) N.

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key is \(8.355\times10^{-5}\) T. From \(I = 5.2\) A at \(d = 3.1\) cm, \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d} = \dfrac{2\times10^{-7}\times 5.2}{0.031} = 3.355\times10^{-5}\) T. Every digit after the first agrees with the correct value, so the printed key differs from it only in its leading digit — 8 where 3 belongs.]

Given: \(I = 5.2\) A, \(d = 3.1\) cm \(= 0.031\) m, \(\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\) T m/A.

For a very long straight wire,
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d} = \dfrac{2\times10^{-7}\times 5.2}{0.031} = \dfrac{1.04\times10^{-6}}{0.031}\)
\(\therefore B = 3.355\times10^{-5}\) T

(The field is tangential to the circle of radius 3.1 cm drawn round the wire, in the sense given by the right-hand grip rule.)

[Textbook misprint: the question reads "the force per unit length on each of the wires in \(4.76\times10^{-2}\) N". A force per unit length carries units of \(\text{N m}^{-1}\), not N, and the word should be "is". The value is used above as \(4.76\times10^{-2}\) N/m, which is what reproduces the book's own printed answer of 56.68 A.]

Given: separation \(d = 1.35\) cm \(= 1.35\times10^{-2}\) m, force per unit length \(\dfrac{F}{L} = 4.76\times10^{-2}\) N/m, equal currents \(I\) in both wires.

The force per unit length between two long parallel current-carrying wires is
\(\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I^{2}}{2\pi d}\)   (since \(I_1 = I_2 = I\))
\(\therefore I^{2} = \dfrac{(F/L)\,2\pi d}{\mu_0} = \dfrac{4.76\times10^{-2}\times 1.35\times10^{-2}}{2\times10^{-7}} = 3.213\times10^{3}\)
\(\therefore I = \sqrt{3213} = 56.68\) A

Given: \(d = 2.4\) cm \(= 0.024\) m, \(B = 16\ \mu\)T \(= 16\times10^{-6}\) T.

For a long straight wire, \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}\), so
\(I = \dfrac{2\pi d\,B}{\mu_0} = \dfrac{B\,d}{2\times10^{-7}} = \dfrac{16\times10^{-6}\times 0.024}{2\times10^{-7}} = \dfrac{3.84\times10^{-7}}{2\times10^{-7}}\)
\(\therefore I = 1.92\) A

Given: \(R = 12.3\) cm \(= 0.123\) m, \(B = 6.4\times10^{-6}\) T at the centre, single turn.

**Step 1 — find the current.** At the centre of a circular loop,
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}\)
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{2RB}{\mu_0} = \dfrac{2\times 0.123\times 6.4\times10^{-6}}{4\pi\times10^{-7}} = \dfrac{1.574\times10^{-6}}{1.2566\times10^{-6}}\)
\(\therefore I = 1.253\) A

**Step 2 — magnetic moment.** For a plane current loop \(m = IA = I\pi R^{2}\):
\(m = 1.253 \times \pi \times (0.123)^{2} = 1.253 \times 0.04753\)
\(\therefore m = 5.954\times10^{-2}\) A m\(^2\)

The magnetic moment is directed along the axis of the loop, in the sense given by the right-hand rule applied to the circulating current.

Given: \(R = 9.7\) cm \(= 0.097\) m, \(I = 2.3\) A, single turn.

**(a) At the centre of the loop.**
\(B_{centre} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R} = \dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times 2.3}{2\times 0.097} = \dfrac{2.890\times10^{-6}}{0.194}\)
\(\therefore B_{centre} = 1.49\times10^{-5}\) T

**(b) On the axis, at \(x = 9.7\) cm from the centre.** For a point on the axis of a circular loop,
\(B_{axis} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^{2}}{2\,(R^{2}+x^{2})^{3/2}}\)
Here \(x = R\), so \(R^{2}+x^{2} = 2R^{2}\) and \((2R^{2})^{3/2} = 2\sqrt{2}\,R^{3}\):
\(B_{axis} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^{2}}{2\times 2\sqrt{2}R^{3}} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\sqrt{2}\,R} = \dfrac{B_{centre}}{2\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{1.49\times10^{-5}}{2.828}\)
\(\therefore B_{axis} = 5.27\times10^{-6}\) T

So moving one radius along the axis reduces the field by the factor \(2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.83\). Both fields point along the axis of the loop.

Given: \(N = 100\) turns, \(R = 8.0\) cm \(= 0.08\) m, \(I = 0.40\) A.

Each turn contributes equally at the centre, so
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{2R} = \dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times 100 \times 0.40}{2\times 0.08} = \dfrac{5.027\times10^{-5}}{0.16}\)
\(\therefore B = 3.142\times10^{-4}\) T

The field is directed along the axis of the coil, in the sense given by the right-hand rule.

[Textbook misprint: the question does not supply the proton mass, which the calculation requires. The standard value \(m_p = 1.67\times10^{-27}\) kg — the value this book's own Q.17 supplies for the same particle — is used above, and it reproduces the printed answer.]

Given: \(B = 1.4\) Wb/m\(^2\), protons (mass \(m = 1.67\times10^{-27}\) kg, charge \(e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\) C).

Inside a dee the proton moves on a circle whose period is independent of its speed and radius:
\(T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{eB} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 1.67\times10^{-27}}{1.6\times10^{-19}\times 1.4} = \dfrac{1.049\times10^{-26}}{2.24\times10^{-19}}\)
\(\therefore T = 4.684\times10^{-8}\) s

The proton crosses the gap between the two dees **twice** per revolution, so the accelerating electric field must reverse once every **half** period:
\(t = \dfrac{T}{2} = \dfrac{4.684\times10^{-8}}{2}\)
\(\therefore t = 2.342\times10^{-8}\) s

This is the time period for reversing the electric field between the two dees.

Given: \(N = 50\) turns, coil \(5\) cm \(\times\) \(3\) cm so \(A = 0.05\times 0.03 = 1.5\times10^{-3}\) m\(^2\), radial field \(B = 0.05\) Wb/m\(^2\), torsional constant \(k = 1.5\times10^{-9}\) Nm/degree, deflection \(\theta = 30^\circ\).

In a moving coil galvanometer the radial field keeps the coil plane always parallel to \(\vec{B}\), so the deflecting torque is \(NIAB\) at every position. At equilibrium it is balanced by the restoring torque \(k\theta\) of the suspension:
\(NIAB = k\theta\)
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{k\theta}{NAB} = \dfrac{1.5\times10^{-9}\times 30}{50 \times 1.5\times10^{-3}\times 0.05} = \dfrac{4.5\times10^{-8}}{3.75\times10^{-3}}\)
\(\therefore I = 1.2\times10^{-5}\) A

(Because \(k\) is quoted per **degree**, \(\theta\) is used in degrees and no conversion to radians is needed.)

Given: length \(L = \pi\) m, diameter 5 cm, \(N = 1000\) turns, \(I = 5\) A.

Number of turns per unit length:
\(n = \dfrac{N}{L} = \dfrac{1000}{\pi}\) turns/m

For a long solenoid the field at the centre, on the axis, is
\(B = \mu_0 n I = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\times \dfrac{1000}{\pi}\times 5 = 4\times10^{-7}\times 1000 \times 5\)
\(\therefore B = 2\times10^{-3}\) T

The \(\pi\) in \(\mu_0\) cancels against the \(\pi\) in the length. Note that the diameter does not enter: for an ideal (long) solenoid the axial field depends only on \(n\) and \(I\), and the 5 cm diameter merely confirms that the solenoid is long compared with its width. The field is directed along the axis.

Given: mean radius \(r = 10\) cm \(= 0.10\) m, \(N = 1000\) turns, \(B = 5\times10^{-2}\) T along the axis of the toroid.

Applying Ampere's law to a circular Amperian loop of radius \(r\) along the axis of the winding, the loop encloses all \(N\) turns:
\(B\,(2\pi r) = \mu_0 N I\)
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{B\,2\pi r}{\mu_0 N} = \dfrac{5\times10^{-2}\times 2\pi \times 0.10}{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times 1000} = \dfrac{3.1416\times10^{-2}}{1.2566\times10^{-3}}\)
\(\therefore I = 25\) A

Given: radius of the dee \(R = 60\) cm \(= 0.60\) m, oscillator frequency \(f = 10\) MHz \(= 10^{7}\) Hz, proton mass \(m = 1.67\times10^{-27}\) kg, \(e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\) C, 1 eV \(= 1.6\times10^{-19}\) J.

The proton leaves the cyclotron at the rim of the dee, where its orbit radius is \(R\). The oscillator frequency equals the cyclotron frequency \(f = v/2\pi R\), so the maximum speed is
\(v = 2\pi f R = 2\pi \times 10^{7}\times 0.60\)
\(\therefore v = 3.77\times10^{7}\) m/s

Hence the kinetic energy on ejection:
\(KE = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\times 1.67\times10^{-27}\times (3.77\times10^{7})^{2}\)
\(\therefore KE = 1.187\times10^{-12}\) J
\(\therefore KE = \dfrac{1.187\times10^{-12}}{1.6\times10^{-19}} = 7.42\times10^{6}\) eV \(= 7.42\) MeV

The loop is made of two parts, both of which lie in the plane of the page and both of which have P as their reference point.

**Segment I — the circular arc.** It is an arc of radius \(R\) centred at P subtending \(270^\circ = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\) radians. For a circular arc of angle \(\theta\) at its centre,
\(B_{I} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}\theta = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}\times\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\)

**Segment II — the straight portion.** Its contribution is given in the question:
\(B_{II} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}\sqrt{2}\)

**Direction.** Applying the right-hand rule to each part: the current runs clockwise round the arc as drawn, and the straight segment lies below P with its current directed to the left. For both, \(\mathrm{d}\vec{l}\times\hat{r}\) points **into the plane of the page**, so the two contributions are parallel and simply add.

\(B = B_{I} + B_{II} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}\left[\dfrac{3\pi}{2} + \sqrt{2}\right]\)

Numerically \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} + \sqrt{2} = 4.712 + 1.414 = 6.127\), so \(B = 6.127\,\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}\), directed **perpendicular to the plane of the loop and into the page**.

Let the two wires be a distance \(R\) apart, each carrying a current \(I\) into the plane of the page. Take the origin at the midpoint of the line joining them, the \(x\)-axis along that line and the \(y\)-axis perpendicular to it, so the wires sit at \(x = \pm R/2\).

P is equidistant from both wires and subtends an angle \(\theta\) with the plane containing them, so P lies on the perpendicular bisector at
\(y = \dfrac{R}{2}\tan\theta\),   and its distance from each wire is   \(d = \dfrac{R}{2\cos\theta}\)

**Field of one wire.** Each wire produces \(B_1 = B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}\), directed perpendicular to the line joining that wire to P (tangent to the circle centred on the wire).

**Resolving.** By symmetry the two fields make equal angles with the \(x\)-axis on opposite sides. Their components **perpendicular** to the line joining the wires are equal and opposite and cancel; the components **parallel** to that line add. Each parallel component is \(B_1\cos\alpha\) where \(\alpha\) is the angle between \(\vec{B}_1\) and the \(x\)-axis, and geometry gives \(\cos\alpha = y/d\). Hence
\(B = 2\,\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}\times\dfrac{y}{d} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{\pi}\dfrac{y}{d^{2}}\)

**Substituting.** \(y = \dfrac{R}{2}\tan\theta\) and \(d^{2} = \dfrac{R^{2}}{4\cos^{2}\theta}\), so
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{\pi}\times\dfrac{R\tan\theta}{2}\times\dfrac{4\cos^{2}\theta}{R^{2}} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{\pi R}\times 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\)
\(\therefore B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{\pi}\dfrac{I}{R}\sin 2\theta\)   (using \(2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \sin 2\theta\))

which is the required result.

**Direction.** The resultant is **parallel to the line joining the two wires** (i.e. it lies in the plane containing them and is perpendicular to the wires themselves). With both currents into the page and P on the far side of the wire-plane, the right-hand grip rule gives the same sense for both wires, and that common component is what survives.

A numerical check of the two expressions at \(\theta = 10^\circ, 30^\circ, 45^\circ, 70^\circ\) (with \(R = 0.4\) m, \(I = 7\) A) shows them agreeing to every digit.

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key is \(B = \dfrac{J_0\mu_0 r}{3a}\), which is dimensionally impossible for a magnetic field — \((\text{T m A}^{-1})(\text{A m}^{-2})(\text{m})/(\text{m})\) reduces to \(\text{T m}^{-1}\), not T. Integrating the given \(J = J_0 r/a\) over the enclosed area gives \(I_{enclosed} = \dfrac{2\pi J_0 r^{3}}{3a}\) and hence \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 J_0 r^{2}}{3a}\); the printed key has lost the square on \(r\).]

Given: current density \(J = \dfrac{J_0 r}{a}\), directed along the axis of the wire.

Choose a circular Amperian loop of radius \(r\) coaxial with the wire and lying inside it. Because \(J\) varies with radius, the enclosed current must be found by integration over annular rings of radius \(r'\) and thickness \(\mathrm{d}r'\), each of area \(2\pi r'\,\mathrm{d}r'\):

\(I_{enclosed} = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{r} J\,(2\pi r')\,\mathrm{d}r' = \int_{0}^{r}\dfrac{J_0 r'}{a}\,2\pi r'\,\mathrm{d}r' = \dfrac{2\pi J_0}{a}\int_{0}^{r} r'^{2}\,\mathrm{d}r'\)
\(\therefore I_{enclosed} = \dfrac{2\pi J_0}{a}\times\dfrac{r^{3}}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi J_0 r^{3}}{3a}\)

By symmetry \(B\) has the same magnitude everywhere on the loop and is tangential to it, so Ampere's law gives
\(B\,(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I_{enclosed} = \mu_0\dfrac{2\pi J_0 r^{3}}{3a}\)
\(\therefore B = \dfrac{\mu_0 J_0 r^{2}}{3a}\)

The field is tangential — it circles the axis of the wire, in the sense given by the right-hand grip rule.

A dimensional check confirms the result: \([\mu_0][J_0][r^{2}]/[a] = (\text{T m A}^{-1})(\text{A m}^{-2})(\text{m}^{2})/(\text{m}) = \text{T}\), and a direct numerical integration of \(I_{enclosed}\) reproduces this expression exactly at \(r = 0.01, 0.02\) and \(0.04\) m.

Here the current density \(J\) is **uniform** across the cross-section, so no integration is needed: the current enclosed by a coaxial Amperian loop of radius \(r\) inside the wire is simply \(J\) times the area of that loop.

\(I_{enclosed} = J \times \pi r^{2}\)

Applying Ampere's law to that loop, on which \(B\) is constant in magnitude and everywhere tangential:
\(B\,(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I_{enclosed} = \mu_0 J \pi r^{2}\)
\(\therefore B = \dfrac{\mu_0 J r}{2}\)

So for a uniform current density the field grows **linearly** with \(r\) inside the wire, whereas in the previous problem, where \(J\) itself increased linearly with \(r\), the field grew as \(r^{2}\). The direction is tangential, circling the axis in the sense given by the right-hand grip rule.
